clue.text: False rumour an eccentric put about

parts.note: a card is an eccentric or amusing person
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone notes that a lie is being spread by an odd character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eccentric' looks like an adjective but is a noun here: in British usage a card is a comic oddball.
explanation.definitionFit: A canard is an unfounded story or hoax deliberately circulated.

clue.text: Thirty days in Capri left

indicators.note: the letters are found inside the word Capri, dropping its first letter

parts.note: the letters sitting within the name

explanation.surface: A month-long stay spent on the Italian island of Capri, then departing.
explanation.walkthrough: APRI sits inside CAPRI; L for 'left' finishes it.
explanation.definitionFit: The month in question has thirty days, as the rhyme 'Thirty days hath September, April, June and November' recalls.

clue.text: Pets aren't barking just now

indicators.note: barking is British slang for mad, so the letters of the words go crazy and rearrange

explanation.surface: The animals are quiet for the moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barking' looks like what pets do, but in British slang it means mad, signalling the rearrangement; the apostrophe is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases mean currently, at this moment in time.

clue.text: Finish first of games on hole that bends sharply

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word games is taken

parts.note: its opening letter
in cricket the on side is also called the leg side

explanation.surface: A golfer finishes the round on a sharply curving hole.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket convention that the on side is the LEG side supplies the last part.
explanation.definitionFit: In golf a dogleg is a fairway with a sharp bend, like a dog's hind leg.

clue.text: Group of musicians — see men playing around British Legion

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go around the abbreviation for the veterans' charity
the words see men are playing about, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
BL is the abbreviation for the British Legion, a UK charity for ex-servicemen

explanation.surface: An invitation to watch a band performing at a British Legion club.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of SEE MEN goes around BL; the British Legion is a UK veterans' charity with social clubs.
explanation.definitionFit: An ensemble is a small group of musicians who perform together.

clue.text: Answering me, they ruffled American author

indicators.note: the words are ruffled, disturbed and messed up, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is upset that a group replied to them.
explanation.definitionFit: Ernest Hemingway was the US novelist who wrote The Old Man and the Sea.

clue.text: Madness, regularly wearing fancy gowns for final act

the gowns are made fancy, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: taking letters at regular intervals from Madness

parts.note: every other letter, starting with the second

explanation.surface: It is madness for performers to wear elaborate gowns for the last number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Madness' looks like comment on the scene, but 'regularly' takes its second, fourth and sixth letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A swan song is a person's last performance or achievement, from the legend that swans sing before dying.

clue.text: Fielder, Mike I assume

parts.note: Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet
to don clothes is to put them on, assume them

explanation.surface: A man called Mike guesses he is fielding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Assume' looks like 'suppose' but means put on, as clothing. Mid-on is a cricket fielding position on the leg side.
explanation.definitionFit: Mid-on is a cricket fielding position, so it names a fielder stationed there.

clue.text: Stable worker, guy after special uniform

parts.note: livery is distinctive uniform worn by servants or company members
a guy is a man

explanation.surface: A stable hand gets special uniform for a chap.
explanation.walkthrough: A livery stable keeps horses for owners or hires them out.
explanation.definitionFit: A liveryman can be someone who keeps or works at a livery stable, looking after horses.

clue.text: Promotional material must have right look, it's said

parts.note: right is proper; a gander is a look, as in 'have a gander'

explanation.surface: Advertising copy must have the correct appearance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Have a gander' is British slang for take a look; in a non-rhotic British accent 'proper gander' sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Propaganda is biased material spread to promote a cause or point of view.

clue.text: Daughter and I very edgy, initially, in disreputable bar

parts.note: first letter
first letter; the run of letters across 'and I very' is a coincidence, not the setter's device
first letter
first letter

explanation.surface: A daughter and her parent feel nervous in a seedy pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A dive is slang for a shabby, rundown drinking place or club.

clue.text: Baffled, as Clouseau often was?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: the bumbling film detective was often without a clue

explanation.walkthrough: Inspector Clouseau of the Pink Panther films is a hopeless detective, so he frequently lacks clues in both senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Clueless means having no idea, puzzled and bewildered.

clue.text: Guard southern passageway

parts.note: an entry is a passage or way in

explanation.surface: A guard stands at a passage in the south.
explanation.definitionFit: A sentry is a soldier posted to keep watch, a guard.

clue.text: Primate crossing small part of church

indicators.note: the ape is across, i.e. straddling, the letter for small

parts.note: an ape is a primate
S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: A monkey wanders across a little section of a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Primate' could mean an archbishop in a church scene, but here it is the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is the semicircular recess at the end of a church, usually behind the altar.

clue.text: Head of possum, strange arboreal animal

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: its opening letter

indicators.note: the letters of arboreal are made strange, rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A possum's head peeps from a weird tree-dwelling creature.
explanation.definitionFit: The polar bear is a large white Arctic mammal, the creature meant here.

clue.text: Hotel, even more attractive

parts.note: Hotel is H in the NATO phonetic alphabet
'and some' is an idiom meaning and even more

explanation.surface: A hotel that is more appealing still.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And some' is a colloquial way of saying 'and even more' (it was cold, and some).
explanation.definitionFit: Handsome means good-looking, pleasing in appearance.

clue.text: Facial hair of border poet

parts.note: a side is an edge or border
Robert Burns was the Scottish national poet

explanation.surface: The beard of a poet who lives on the border.
explanation.definitionFit: Sideburns are strips of hair grown down a man's cheeks in front of the ears.

clue.text: Northern name full of love and understanding? Rubbish!

indicators.note: the two letters are full of, i.e. contain, the love letter

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like O
sense is good judgement or understanding

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs at a northerner's name supposedly full of love and empathy.
explanation.walkthrough: N and N hold O, giving NON, then SENSE follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Nonsense is a dismissive exclamation, like 'Rubbish!', meaning what was said is foolish.

clue.text: Policy of factory rejecting new mould

indicators.note: the word for factory rejects, i.e. throws out, the letter for new

parts.note: a plant is an industrial factory
to form something is to mould it

explanation.surface: A factory's policy is to discard fresh casts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Policy' is the definition in its political sense; 'rejecting' throws out the abbreviation for new.
explanation.definitionFit: A platform is a political party's declared set of policies.

clue.text: Have a meal in Madrid, inexpensive

indicators.note: the answer is held in the run of letters across the two words

explanation.surface: A suggestion to eat cheaply in the Spanish capital.
explanation.definitionFit: To dine is to eat dinner, a formal word for eating a meal.

clue.text: Editor, following troublesome situation, gets drunk

indicators.note: the editor's letters come following the word for trouble

parts.note: to be in a stew is to be in a troublesome situation

explanation.surface: An editor in a fix after a crisis takes to the bottle.
explanation.definitionFit: Stewed is slang for intoxicated, as in being pickled or sozzled.

clue.text: Free renegade held by US soldiers

parts.note: GIs are American soldiers
a rat is someone who deserts or betrays, a renegade

explanation.surface: A turncoat is released after being captured by American troops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free' looks like a verb for the release, but the answer is the adjective meaning without charge.
explanation.definitionFit: Gratis means without payment, at no cost.

clue.text: Herb helping to make healthy meal

indicators.note: helping to make says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A herb that goes into preparing a nutritious dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: Thyme is an aromatic culinary plant used to season food.

clue.text: College backing up reserve computer

parts.note: Eton College is the famous English public school
to book is to reserve

explanation.surface: A college keeps a spare computer as a backup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing up' borrows computer jargon for the reversal; Eton is an elite English boarding school.
explanation.definitionFit: A notebook is a small portable laptop computer.

clue.text: Second article in gold

parts.note: or is the heraldic word for gold
the is the definite article

explanation.surface: A second piece made of gold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' is an adjective here: the other one, the alternative.
explanation.definitionFit: Other can mean second or alternative, as in 'every other day'.

clue.text: Refuse in private room close to study

indicators.note: the close, or end, of the word study

parts.note: its final letter

explanation.surface: Rubbish piled up in a private room near the study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' reads as a noun, rubbish, but the answer is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To deny is to refuse or withhold something requested.

clue.text: Topical story, when released, about whiskey

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go about the letter for whiskey
the words are released, set loose, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
Whiskey is W in the NATO phonetic alphabet

clue.text: Leaves railway behind English writer

parts.note: Graham Greene was an English novelist

explanation.surface: An English author departs, leaving the railway behind.

clue.text: Leave course having lost heart
